candidates.title: List of chemistry mnemonics
candidates.text:
A mnemonic is a memory aid used to improve long-term memory and make the process of consolidation easier. Many chemistry aspects, rules, names of compounds, sequences of elements, their reactivity, etc., can be easily and efficiently memorized with the help of mnemonics. This article contains the list of certain mnemonics in chemistry.

A redox reaction is a chemical reaction in which there is a change in oxidation state of atoms participating in the reaction.

An atom (or ion) whose oxidation number increases in a redox reaction is said to be oxidized (and is called a reducing agent). It is accomplished by loss of one or more electrons. The atom whose oxidation number decreases gains (receives) one or more electrons and is said to be reduced. This relation can be remembered by the following mnemonics.

candidates.title: Silanes
candidates.text:
In organosilicon chemistry, silanes are a diverse class of charge-neutral organic compounds with the general formula SiR. The R substituents can be any combination of organic or inorganic groups. Most silanes contain Si-C bonds, and are discussed under organosilicon compounds. Some contain Si-H bonds and are discussed under hydrosilanes.

Silane SiH, the parent.

Binary silicon-hydrogen compounds (which are sometimes called silanes also) includes silane itself but also compounds with Si-Si bonds including disilane and longer chains.

Silanes with one, two, three, or four Si-H bonds are called hydrosilanes. Silane is again the parent member. Examples: triethylsilane (HSi(C H)) and triethoxysilane (HSi(OC H)).

Polysilanes are organosilicon compounds with the formula (R Si). They feature Si-Si bonds. Attracting more interest are the organic derivatives such as polydimethylsilane ((CH) Si). Dodecamethylcyclohexasilane ((CH) Si) is an oligomer of such materials. Formally speaking, polysilanes also include compounds of the type (SiH)n, but these less studied.

Carbosilanes are polymeric silanes with alternating Si-C bonds.

Chlorosilanes have Si-Cl bonds. The dominant examples come from the Direct process, i.e., (CH) SiCl. Another important member is trichlorosilane (SiHCl).

Organosilanes are a class of charge-neutral organosilicon compounds. Example: tetramethylsilane (Si(CH))

By tradition, compounds with Si-O-Si bonds are usually not referred to as silanes. Instead, they are called siloxanes. One example is hexamethyldisiloxane, ((CH) Si) O.

Compound-specific applications are:

Polysilicone production

PEX crosslinking agent

Textile finishing industry

Dentistry

Integrated in battery materials to longevity

Construction materials (Acryloxy Silane)

candidates.title: Group 14 hydride
candidates.text:
Group 14 hydrides are chemical compounds composed of hydrogen atoms and group 14 atoms (the elements of group 14 are carbon, silicon, germanium, tin, lead and flerovium).

The tetrahydride series has the chemical formula XH, with X representing any of the carbon family. Methane is commonly the result of the decomposition of organic matter and is a greenhouse gas. The other hydrides are generally unstable, poisonous metal hydrides.

They take on a pyramidal structure, and as such are not polar molecules like the other p-block hydrides.

Unlike other light hydrides such as ammonia, water and hydrogen fluoride, methane does not exhibit any anomalous effects attributed to hydrogen bonding, and so its properties conform well to the prevailing trend of heavier group 14 hydrides.

This series has the chemical formula X H. Ethane is commonly found alongside methane in natural gas. The other hydrides of the chemical formula X H are less stable than the corresponding tetrahydrides XH, and they are more and more less stable as X goes from carbon (ethane C H is stable) down to lead (or flerovium) in the periodic table (diplumbane Pb H is unknown).

All straight-chain saturated group 14 hydrides follow the formula X H, the same formula for the alkanes.

Many other group 14 hydrides are known. Carbon forms a huge variety of hydrocarbons (among the simplest alkanes are methane CH, ethane C H, propane C H, butane C H, pentane C H and hexane C H, with a wide range of uses. There is also polyethylene (CH), where n is very large, a stable hydrocarbon polymer, the most commonly produced plastic. Hydrocarbons also include alkenes, which contain a double bond between carbon atoms (e.g. ethylene H C=CH), alkynes, which contain a triple bond between carbon atoms (e.g. acetylene H−C≡C−H), cyclic and branched hydrocarbons (e.g. cyclohexane C H, limonene C H, which is a cyclic hydrocarbon with double bonds between carbon atoms, and neopentane C(CH), which is a branched hydrocarbon), as well as aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzene C H and toluene C H −CH), whose study forms the core of organic chemistry.

Alongside hydrogen, carbon can form compounds with the chemically similar halogens, forming haloalkanes. The simplest of this series, the halomethanes, contain compounds such as dichloromethane CH Cl, chloroform CHCl and iodoform CHI. Other such important chemicals include vinyl chloride H C=CHCl, which is used in the production of PVC.

The other group 14 elements have a lower tendency to catenate. Hydrosilicons (binary silicon-hydrogen compounds), a silicon analogs of hydrocarbons, such as silanes Si H are known for n = 1–8, in which thermal stability decreasing as n increases (e.g. silane SiH and disilane Si H), as are cyclosilanes (e.g. cyclopentasilane Si H and cyclohexasilane Si H). They are very reactive, pyrophoric colourless gases or volatile liquids. Their volatility is intermediate between the alkanes and the germanes. Unsaturated silanes, the silenes and silynes, have been characterized spectroscopically. The first members of each respectively are disilene H Si=SiH and disilyne H−Si≡Si−H, the silicon analogues of ethylene and acetylene respectively.

The first five hydrogermaniums Ge H are known and are fairly similar to the hydrosilicones, e.g. germane GeH and digermane Ge H. They are germanium analogues of alkanes.

Stannane SnH, a strong reducing agent slowly decomposes at room temperature to tin and hydrogen gas, and is decomposed by concentrated aqueous acids or alkalis; distannane, Sn H is still more unstable, and longer hydrostannums (hydrotins) are unknown. Stannane and distannane are tin analogues of methane and ethane respectively.

Plumbane PbH is very poorly characterised and is only known in trace amounts: even at low temperatures, synthesis methods that yield the other MH compounds fail to give PbH. No other hydroplumbums (hydroleads) are known. However, some substituted diplumbanes, with a general chemical formula R Pb−PbR are more stable, where the R groups are organyl.

Compounds containing hydrogen and multiple group 14 elements are known, one of the most famous of these being tetraethyllead Pb(CH CH) which contains carbon and lead. The other examples are methylsilane H C−SiH which contains carbon and silicon, tris(trimethylsilyl)germanium hydride ((CH) Si) GeH which contain carbon, silicon and germanium, silylgermane or germylsilane H Si−GeH which contains silicon and germanium, and hexaphenyldiplumbane (C H) Pb−Pb(C H) which contains carbon and lead.
